title: A while loop that never moves
summary: Learn why a while loop can run forever when its condition variable does not move toward making the condition false.
objectives: Explain why a `while` loop can keep running when its condition stays `true`.
Trace a loop to see whether its condition variable changes.
Update a variable in a way that moves it toward ending the loop.
Recognise loops that fail to end because a variable moves in the wrong direction or an update is skipped.

blocks.text: A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. This loop tests whether `i` is less than `5`, but never changes `i`:
Because `i` stays at `0`, the condition `i < 5` stays `true`. The loop keeps printing `0` and does not end. This is an infinite loop: a loop that keeps running without stopping.

blocks.title: Compile time and run time
blocks.text: Java accepts this loop when it is inside a valid method. It compiles without a warning about the loop. The problem happens at run time: the program keeps running instead of reaching the code after the loop.

sections.title: Why the loop does not stop

blocks.text: Before each pass, Java checks the condition. If it is `true`, Java runs the body and checks again. To make this loop stop, the body must change `i` so that it eventually reaches a value where `i < 5` is `false`.

blocks.caption: A loop checks its condition before each pass
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start with i = 0]) --> B{i < 5?}
  B -- yes --> C[Run the body]
  C --> D[Change i to i + 1]
  D --> B
  B -- no --> E([Loop ends])

blocks.text: The diagram includes the needed change, `i = i + 1`. Without it, the path returns to the condition with the same value of `i`. The condition remains `true` forever.

blocks.title: Three things to check
items: Which variable does the condition test? Here it is `i`.
Does the loop body change that variable? Here it needs to change `i`.
Does the change move the variable toward making the condition `false`? With `i < 5`, adding `1` moves `i` toward `5`.

sections.title: Trace it, one pass at a time

blocks.text: A trace is a record of what happens in each pass. Follow the broken loop and write down the value of `i` each time Java checks `i < 5`.

blocks.caption: Tracing the loop that never updates i

blocks.text: The same thing happens at every later check. There is no next value for `i`, so the condition never gets a chance to become `false`.

sections.title: Worked examples: add the right change

blocks.text: For a loop to end, its update must move the condition variable toward a value that makes the condition `false`. Here are two complete programs with that update in place.

good.title: Add 1 on every pass

blocks.note: In the complete program, `i++` adds `1` to `i` after each print. The values reach `5`, and then `i < 5` is `false`, so the loop ends.

good.title: Subtract 1 on every pass

blocks.note: Here `remaining--` subtracts `1`. The values move from `3` to `2`, then `1`, then `0`. At `0`, the condition `remaining > 0` is `false`.

blocks.caption: Body executions in the two corrected examples

blocks.text: The update can be present and the loop can still fail to end. Check that the update moves in the right direction and that it actually runs on every pass.

blocks.note: In the first loop, `i--` makes `i` smaller, so `i < 5` stays `true`. In the second, `i++` makes `i` larger until the condition becomes `false`.

blocks.text: A `continue` statement skips the rest of the current pass and jumps to the next condition check. If the update comes after a `continue`, that pass may skip the update. For example, when `i` reaches `2` in this loop, it never changes again:

Floating-point values can also cause a loop to miss its target. Rounding can make a value step past an exact target, so a condition such as `value != 1.0` may stay `true`. Do not rely on exact floating-point equality to end a loop.

blocks.title: Check every route through the body
blocks.text: Follow the body from top to bottom. Ask whether every route reaches the update before the next condition check. A `continue` can skip an update placed later in the body.

blocks.question: What happens when this loop runs?
blocks.explanation: The body never changes `i`, so `i` stays `0` and `i < 3` stays `true`. The Java compiler accepts the loop, but it keeps running when the program runs.

blocks.question: Which update makes this loop end?
blocks.explanation: The condition is `count > 0`. Subtracting `1` moves `count` toward `0`, where the condition becomes `false`.

blocks.question: Why can this loop get stuck when `i` reaches `2`?
options: The loop condition is checked only once.
blocks.explanation: `continue` skips the rest of that pass. At `i == 2`, the loop jumps back to its condition without running `i++`, so `i` remains `2` and `i < 5` remains `true`.

items: A `while` loop repeats while its condition is `true`.
Change the variable tested by the condition inside the loop body.
Make the change move toward a value that makes the condition `false`.
A loop can compile without warning and still run forever.
Check that every route through the body reaches the update; `continue` can skip code later in the body.
Avoid exact floating-point equality as a loop-ending condition because rounding can step past the target.
